The best AI agent orchestration platforms in 2026 are Temporal for durable execution, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for AWS teams, and Microsoft Foundry Agent Service for Microsoft 365 shops, with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, IBM watsonx Orchestrate, Orkes, and CrewAI Enterprise covering Google Cloud, cross-vendor governance, workflow-first teams, and CrewAI users. An orchestration platform is the runtime that schedules, retries, monitors, and recovers agents once real traffic hits them, which is a different job from the framework you write agent code in.
Last verified: October 2026

Most "best AI agent framework" lists mix the two together. That is how teams pick LangGraph or CrewAI as a library, reach production, and then discover they still need a deployment and orchestration layer on top. This guide only covers that second layer. If you want the libraries, see our best multi-agent frameworks comparison. If you want model routing, gateways, and LLM observability, see the best LLM orchestration tools guide or the open-source LLM orchestration and routing tools roundup. None of the seven platforms below appear in those posts.

A note on how new this category is: the three hyperscaler products here are recent. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore reached general availability on October 13, 2025. Microsoft announced the rename of Azure AI Foundry to Microsoft Foundry at Ignite in November 2025. Google announced the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform as the successor to Vertex AI on April 22, 2026. None of them carry the years of independent review volume a mature category like RPA has, so this guide cites vendor documentation and published rate cards instead of ratings.
How we compared these AI agent orchestration platforms
Four criteria:
What it actually orchestrates. Does it schedule and recover multi-step agent execution in production, or is it a library you import into your own runtime?
Pricing transparency. A published rate card, even a consumption-based one, versus "contact sales" as the only answer.
Current, not historical, positioning. Several of these products were renamed in 2025 and 2026. This guide uses the names and scope shown on each vendor's site in October 2026.
Real deployment signal. GA status, named customers on the vendor's own site, and documentation depth, since review-count comparisons don't work cleanly yet in a category this new.

1. Temporal, best for durable execution of long-running agent workflows

Temporal is a durable execution platform that ran production workflows (payments, order processing, infrastructure automation) before "agent orchestration" was a category, and it now leads with AI. Its homepage headline in October 2026 reads "The world's best AI runs on Temporal" and names OpenAI, Lovable, Replit, Cursor, and Retool. The idea maps directly to agents: a Temporal Workflow can call an LLM, wait on a tool result, retry a failed step, or pause for days without losing state.

Temporal's pricing page lists durable AI agent support in preview, with the OpenAI Agents SDK and Google ADK running LLM and tool calls as durable Activities. The core server is MIT-licensed open source, so you can self-host or use Temporal Cloud.

Best for: engineering teams whose agents run multi-step, long-duration tasks where losing state on a crash or timeout is unacceptable, and who want infrastructure-grade reliability rather than a chat-first agent product.

Pricing: Temporal Cloud is now pay-as-you-go with no base monthly fee, starting at $50 per million actions and dropping to $25 per million self-serve with volume. Active storage is $0.042 per GB-hour and retained storage $0.00105 per GB-hour. New accounts get $150 in credits for 90 days. Support is an add-on: Business starts at the greater of $500/month or 10% of usage (includes 2.5M actions), and Enterprise and Mission Critical are quoted by sales.
Pros:
Durable execution model with years of production use outside AI, so the reliability guarantees are not new
Works with any agent framework or model provider, since it orchestrates at the workflow layer
No features locked behind plan tiers, per its pricing page
Cons:
It is infrastructure, not an agent product, so you still write the agent logic yourself
Actions plus active and retained storage take real modeling to estimate before you commit
2. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, best for a managed, framework-agnostic runtime on AWS

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is AWS's managed platform for deploying and operating AI agents, covering the runtime, memory, identity, gateway, observability, and policy pieces most open-source frameworks leave you to build. AWS describes it as working with any framework, model, or protocol, so agents built with LangGraph, CrewAI, Strands, or custom code can run on it. At GA in October 2025, Runtime added Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol support and Gateway gained the ability to connect to existing MCP servers.
Best for: teams already running production workloads on AWS that want runtime, identity, and memory for agents managed for them, without rebuilding agent logic in a proprietary framework.

Pricing: consumption-based, with a public rate card per component. As of October 2026, Runtime starts at $0.0895 per vCPU-hour and $0.00945 per GB-hour, Gateway costs $0.005 per 1,000 API invocations, Identity is $0.010 per 1,000 token or API key requests (free when used through Runtime or Gateway), and Observability bills at Amazon CloudWatch rates. New AWS customers get up to $200 in Free Tier credits. Several line items are changing in late 2026 (short-term memory moved to per-GB pricing on October 6, 2026), so check the pricing page before you model costs.
Pros:
Framework-agnostic runtime, so no rewrite of existing agent code
Inherits AWS IAM, VPC, and PrivateLink rather than adding another security vendor
One of the most detailed published rate cards in this category
Cons:
The value case depends on the rest of your stack already being on AWS
Many separately metered components (Runtime, Memory, Gateway, Evaluations, Policy) make total cost harder to predict than a single per-action price
3. Microsoft Foundry Agent Service, best for teams standardized on Microsoft 365 and Azure

Foundry Agent Service is the agent runtime inside Microsoft Foundry, the platform Microsoft renamed from Azure AI Foundry at Ignite in November 2025. It hosts agents in a managed, session-isolated runtime with autoscaling and ties them into Entra Agent ID for identity, access control, and lifecycle management. Agents can be published to Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot in one step.

Microsoft's product page says it supports MCP, A2A, and OpenAPI, and that hosted agents can run custom code built with the open-source Microsoft Agent Framework or LangGraph. It also lists connections to "1,400+ MCP-enabled tools" and built-in short-term, long-term, and procedural memory.
Best for: enterprises already running Microsoft 365, Entra ID, and Azure that want agent orchestration to inherit existing identity and compliance controls.

Pricing: consumption-based. Microsoft states that Foundry Agent Service pricing "is based on the individual models and tools you access and use from the service." There is no separate flat subscription.
Pros:
Native Entra ID and Microsoft 365 integration removes an integration step other platforms need
Open protocol support (MCP, A2A, OpenAPI) and bring-your-own-framework hosting
Private networking with bring-your-own VNet for regulated teams
Cons:
Naming has changed twice in two years (Azure AI Studio, Azure AI Foundry, Microsoft Foundry), so older tutorials use outdated names
The value case weakens fast for teams outside the Microsoft ecosystem
4. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, best for teams building on Google Cloud

Google announced the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform at Cloud Next on April 22, 2026, as the successor to Vertex AI. Its documentation uses that name, while the Google Cloud product page now labels it simply "Gemini platform" and says it lets businesses "build, scale, govern and optimize enterprise-grade agents." Agents are built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK), and Google Antigravity is available through the platform for orchestrating multiple agents on a workflow.
The platform offers 200+ Google and third-party models in Model Garden, including Anthropic's Claude family and open models like Gemma.
Best for: teams standardized on Google Cloud and BigQuery that want agent orchestration integrated with their existing data and MLOps tooling.

Pricing: new customers get a $300 Google Cloud free trial credit valid for 90 days. Google also lists a monthly free tier for agent runtimes covering the first 50 vCPU-hours, the first 100 GiB-hours of RAM, and 1 GiB of storage. Beyond that, usage is consumption-based Google Cloud pricing tied to models and compute.
Pros:
Open on model choice (200+ models including non-Google options) rather than Gemini-only
Native BigQuery and Google Cloud MLOps integration
A standing monthly free tier for agent runtimes on top of the one-time credit
Cons:
Two names in circulation (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform in docs, "Gemini platform" on the product page) plus older Vertex AI Agent Builder tutorials make research confusing
Real value depends on being committed to Google Cloud already
5. IBM watsonx Orchestrate, best for cross-vendor governance over agents from multiple sources

IBM watsonx Orchestrate targets a problem the hyperscaler platforms don't solve directly: enterprises with agents built on different frameworks and vendors that need one control plane to see and govern all of them. IBM's product page says it can scan supported third-party agent environments, including Amazon Bedrock, and bring those agents into the watsonx Orchestrate control plane, and it connects through open standards like A2A and MCP.
Best for: large enterprises, particularly regulated industries already using IBM software, that need centralized policy and control across an agent portfolio built by multiple teams.

Pricing: IBM now publishes list prices. As of October 2026 there is a 30-day free trial, Essentials starts at $530/month, Standard starts at $6,360/month, and Premium (data isolation, dedicated data space, HIPAA-ready option) is quoted by sales. Deployment is available on cloud or on premises.
Pros:
Built for cross-vendor governance rather than assuming every agent runs on one company's stack, which matches how agent sprawl happens in large companies
Published entry pricing, so you can budget before a sales call
IBM cites a Leader placement in the IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Agentic AI Platform Software (vendor-cited)
Cons:
The jump from Essentials to Standard is large, so teams that outgrow the entry tier face a big step up
Governance-first positioning makes it a heavier lift than a single-framework platform if you only need one agent workflow in production
6. Orkes (Conductor), best for teams extending existing workflow orchestration to AI agents

Orkes is the commercial platform built on the open-source Conductor workflow engine, which originated at Netflix. It has moved hard toward agents in 2026: Conductor added an AGENT task for calling AI agents from workflows with built-in retries and durability, and a September 2026 Orkes post announced that agents and workflows now run on the same durable engine. For teams already using Conductor-style orchestration for microservices or event-driven systems, agent tasks become one more task type.
Best for: engineering teams that already think in workflow orchestration (distributed tasks, event handlers, human-in-the-loop steps) and want to add LLM and agent tasks inside that model.

Pricing: a free Developer Edition (the FAQ still calls it the Developer Playground) for prototyping, which Orkes says is "not intended or recommended for production use." Enterprise is custom-priced, with Orkes-hosted, customer-hosted, or on-prem deployment and up to a 99.99% availability SLA.
Pros:
Workflow engine with years of production use outside AI, similar reliability logic to Temporal
Deployment flexibility across hosting models for regulated or data-residency-sensitive teams
SOC 2 Type II, RBAC, SSO, and bring-your-own-keys listed on the pricing page
Cons:
The free edition is not production-ready, so a real evaluation requires an Enterprise conversation
Teams without workflow-orchestration experience face a steeper learning curve than agent-first platforms
7. CrewAI Enterprise, best for a hosted control plane over CrewAI-built agent crews

CrewAI the open-source framework (covered in our multi-agent frameworks comparison) is a library for defining agents as role-based team members. CrewAI's paid product, the Enterprise plan (its docs call the managed environment AMP), is the hosted build, deployment, governance, and monitoring layer on top. CrewAI's site describes a Control Plane that "sits in the execution path of every workflow," with tracing of every LLM call, tool call, and memory read, RBAC, audit trails, human-in-the-loop approval gates, and runtime PII redaction.
CrewAI states on its site that it is used by 65% of the Fortune 500. That is a self-reported figure, so treat it as a vendor claim rather than an audited one.
Best for: teams already building with the CrewAI framework that need a managed way to deploy, govern, and monitor those crews in production.

Pricing: the Basic tier is free (visual editor and AI copilot, GitHub integration, 2 agentic workflow automations, 50 workflow executions/month). Enterprise is custom-priced and adds SSO, RBAC, workload identity, PII redaction, deployment on CrewAI cloud, your VPC, or your own infrastructure, and a 45-day onboarding program, with forward deployed engineering available a la carte.
Pros:
The most direct upgrade path for CrewAI framework users, since no framework migration is required
Enterprise adds governance controls (SSO, RBAC, PII redaction) on top of hosting
Agents can be exported as an MCP server or a UI component, per the pricing page
Cons:
The free tier's 50 executions/month makes it a prototyping tier, not a production allowance
Narrower value than the hyperscaler platforms if you are not committed to CrewAI as your framework

How to choose an AI agent orchestration platform
1) Which cloud are you already on?

Your existing cloud is the strongest single predictor of the right pick. AWS shops get the most from AgentCore, Microsoft 365 and Entra ID shops from Foundry Agent Service, and Google Cloud shops from the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Fighting your identity provider costs more than any platform fee.
2) Is the hard problem reliability or governance?

If the pain is agents losing state on long tasks, pick a durable execution engine (Temporal or Orkes). If the pain is dozens of agents built by different teams with no shared policy, pick a governance layer (IBM watsonx Orchestrate, or the control plane of your cloud vendor).
3) Can you model the bill before you commit?

Temporal (per action), AgentCore (per component), and IBM (per plan) publish numbers you can model. Foundry, Gemini, Orkes Enterprise, and CrewAI Enterprise depend on models used or a sales quote. Ask every vendor for a monthly estimate based on your expected agent traffic, not a demo workload.
When a platform is the wrong call

Every platform above assumes a team that can define agent logic, own the integration work, and keep multi-agent systems working once they're live. If that engineering capacity doesn't exist yet, the options are to hire for it or work with a partner that designs and builds the orchestration layer for you.

ManasFlow's AI agent development team builds production agent systems rather than reselling a platform license. For regulated or security-reviewed rollouts, the enterprise AI agents page covers governed, audited deployments. If you're still deciding between a platform and a custom build, the build vs buy AI agents guide walks through that decision.
Red flags when evaluating an agent orchestration platform
"Agentic orchestration" language with no explanation of what happens when a step fails mid-workflow. Ask how the platform handles retries, timeouts, and partial failures, beyond the happy path.
No answer to "which frameworks or models does this lock us into." Some platforms are framework-agnostic; others quietly require the rest of your stack to be on one vendor.
A demo that never shows cost at scale. Every platform on this list bills on usage or capacity in some form.
No mention of identity and governance for agents acting on real systems. An agent that sends emails, modifies records, or spends money needs the same access controls as an employee.
Marketing that implies the platform designs your agent logic. Every platform here still needs a team that defines what the agents do.
FAQ
What is an AI agent orchestration platform?

An AI agent orchestration platform is the production layer that schedules, monitors, retries, and recovers multi-step AI agent execution, as distinct from the framework used to define what an individual agent does. A framework like LangGraph or CrewAI defines agent logic; a platform like Temporal, Bedrock AgentCore, or Foundry Agent Service runs that logic reliably under real traffic.
Is LangGraph an orchestration platform?

No, LangGraph is an open-source framework for building stateful, graph-based agents, not a production orchestration platform on its own. LangChain's hosted deployment layer for LangGraph agents was renamed from LangGraph Platform to LangSmith Deployment in October 2025. Our LLM orchestration tools guide covers LangGraph and LangSmith in detail.
Do I need an orchestration platform if I'm only running one agent?

Usually not yet. These platforms earn their cost when you run multiple agents, multiple workflows, or agents that must survive real production failures (timeouts, partial completions, retries). A single, simple agent often runs fine on a framework alone.
Which AI agent orchestration platform has the most mature production track record?

Temporal and Orkes have the longest track records, because both build on workflow engines that ran production systems before the current AI agent wave. Temporal's homepage cites nine years in production. The hyperscaler products (Bedrock AgentCore, GA in October 2025; Foundry Agent Service; Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, announced April 2026) are newer but integrate more tightly with their clouds.
How much do AI agent orchestration platforms cost?

Most AI agent orchestration platforms bill on usage, and only a few publish full rate cards. As of October 2026, Temporal Cloud starts at $50 per million actions with no base fee, AgentCore Runtime starts at $0.0895 per vCPU-hour, IBM watsonx Orchestrate Essentials starts at $530/month, and CrewAI and Orkes offer free tiers for prototyping with custom Enterprise pricing.
Can I use more than one of these platforms together?

Yes, and it's common. A team might run Temporal or Orkes as the execution engine, build agent logic in an open-source framework, and use a hyperscaler's identity layer for agents that touch sensitive systems. IBM watsonx Orchestrate is designed for this mixed setup, since it can bring agents running on Amazon Bedrock into its own control plane.
The platform doesn't design your agents for you

Every platform on this list can run the multi-agent system you have in mind. The real constraint is usually whether your team has the capacity to design the agent logic, wire up the integrations, and keep the system reliable once it's live, not which vendor's dashboard looks best. If that capacity is the gap, book a 30-minute call to scope what you need before committing to a platform.
